dedupe_keys.name: vaxjo linnaeus canal and lake lagoons for stormwater management sweden

description: This Climate-ADAPT case study describes the Linnaeus canal in Växjö, southern Sweden, an open stormwater canal with sedimentation lagoons built to stop the yearly flooding of Linnégatan street and nearby cellars. A former stream there had been culverted during street construction, and the underground channel lacked capacity after heavy rain; the new open canal restores surface drainage to Växjö Lake, stores water and settles pollutants in lagoons before it reaches the lake, and narrowed the street, improving traffic safety and the townscape. The project ran from 1998 to 2001 and cost nearly 2 million euro, about 15% from the Swedish Local Investment Programme for Sustainable Development and the rest from the city's technical department; Växjö's 2013 adaptation strategy later reviewed its vulnerabilities to heavier rain. The page is free HTML on the Climate-ADAPT portal, sourced from the municipality. Caveats: it was sized for a 10-year rainfall standard before climate change was considered, space limits constrained its dimensions, and monitoring data are not given. It illustrates climate adaptation by retrofitting blue infrastructure for urban drainage; a related record is the EPA National Stormwater Calculator.
name: Växjö Linnaeus canal and lake lagoons for stormwater management (Sweden)
outcomes: An open canal and lagoons built 1998 to 2001 for nearly 2 million euro largely stopped street and cellar flooding after heavy rain and reduced pollutant loads to Växjö Lake.
provider: Climate-ADAPT (European Environment Agency), case study on Växjö municipality
